Game screens: Game screens are the live interface children and leaders see while playing: start page, mission maps, brief cards, choices, feedback, closing cards, Jobs that use this, Talk it over and Break time. Children read them, and many lines are also spoken through read-aloud. Writers must make every action clear in short British English: tap, choose, drag, test, read, run, guide. The screen must never rely on sound alone, colour alone or hidden teacher knowledge. It must respect junior/senior differences, accessibility settings and the fixed day structure. Screens should show evidence, checks and next steps, not long explanations.
Game words (content.js): Game words are the reusable labels, buttons, tooltips, mission titles, lens names, build descriptions and short Florence lines used throughout Eco Town. Children read them constantly while building and checking plans. Writers must preserve exact names such as AI Lab, Flood lens, Street view, Winter test, Walking-time lens, Use Florence’s plan and Back to my town where those names are established. These strings need to be short enough for small screens and read-aloud. They must support the core Eco Town lesson: Florence may be confident, but children check with evidence and clearer instructions.
Story cartoons (voiced): Story cartoons are the short voiced Eco Town episodes before and after each AI Lab mission. Children hear them with captions, and leaders may pause them for questions. They show Florence making a confident but flawed plan, children noticing a problem, a lens or test revealing evidence, and a clearer brief fixing the plan. Writers must keep Florence friendly, scripted and not malicious. The films need memorable question cards, short spoken lines and clear lesson cards. They must not give away the fix too early in opening films. Captions, skip controls and reduced-motion needs matter.
Pages: Pages are the web or surrounding game pages: start, welcome, take-home, visit/share surfaces, passport or printable records where applicable. Children, parents and leaders may read them. Writers must be clear about what is local, what is saved and what is not shared. Do not ask for child names. Do not imply accounts, chat, online galleries or live AI where the material does not support them. The take-home wording should say what the child practised or made, not overclaim learning. The start page must show the six parts in order and only say “about an hour” for parts that truly are.
Leader page: The leader page is for teachers and club leaders running the day. It should explain the timetable, the six-part order, when to pause, where children may get stuck, and how to run screens-down discussion. Leaders need the same Talk it over questions that children see, plus practical prompts about evidence, trade-offs and comparing towns rather than children. Copy must remind leaders that Florence is pretend and scripted, not a live AI. It should also flag privacy, no child names, local sharing rules, accessibility options and the junior no-money rule. Keep it usable during a busy session.
Module: Drone delivery: This area is now the **Drones at work** module, not only delivery. Children work through six real drone jobs: ground school, hand flying, delivery, farm survey, inspection and search and rescue. Writers must keep safety central: pre-flight checks, weather, wind, airspace, Drone Code, fly/do not fly decisions, battery, overlap, safe distance and heat-camera search patterns. Junior wording stays concrete; senior wording can include watt-hours, overlap percentages, side-view height limit and official terms such as Civil Aviation Authority where supplied. Delivery is the built loop inside the wider hour. Avoid fantasy drone uses and do not add money.
Module: Robot training: This area is the **Robots at work** module. Children meet six robot jobs: sense–think–act, robot arm, hospital rules, recycling sorter, weeding robot and flood rescue. Writers must frame robots as systems that sense, decide and act, and children as people who choose sensors, write steps, test rules, label examples, set thresholds and improve designs. Junior wording uses “how sure”, “wrong step” and “make it better”; senior wording can use control loop, centimetres, debugging, classifier, confidence threshold, costs, trade-offs and simulation. There is no typing. Florence’s lines are fixed words, not generated text.
Module: Roads for self-driving cars: This area is the **Self-driving cars** module. Children play six missions about sensing, labelling, road-rule behaviour, simulation testing, shared fleets and street redesign. Writers must avoid making self-driving cars seem perfect. The emphasis is safety, blind spots, edge cases, testable rules, one change at a time, fleet trade-offs and streets that work for passengers, walkers and cyclists. Junior text says self-driving cars and uses plain actions. Senior text can say autonomous cars, fused sensors, recognition model, simulated miles, empty driving and measured outcomes. Mission 6, redesigning the street, is the built loop and leaves the street design in town.
Module: Town film studio: This area is the **Town film studio** module. Children complete six film and media jobs: crew language, storyboarding, directing Florence, editing, access and checking truth/permission. Writers must keep the work practical, not just playful effects. Use real film words such as wide, medium, close-up, pan, tilt, track, storyboard, first cut, feedback, captions and described version, but explain them simply. Florence is a capable AI helper in mission 3; the child briefs her and improves the first cut. Mission 6 must stress checking pictures and asking before filming people. Do not store typed material; mission 3 progress never stores anything typed.
Module: Power control room: This area is the **Power control room** module. Children run six power-system missions: balancing the grid, forecasting, storage, automation rules, smart demand and storm restoration. Writers must keep the tone calm, practical and safety-led. Junior text should use visual ideas such as a level scale, dark squares, spare wind and sun, safe places and bringing everyone back. Senior text can use supply, demand, 50 Hz, kWh, charge/discharge, surplus renewables, constraints, priority load and re-energise. The built loop is automation rules. There is no typing. Records should report measured actions, such as steps balanced, forecasts read, rules tested and priority sites restored.
